fields.claim_quote: the [[Definition:Conditional Probability|conditional probability]] of $A$ given $B$ is $\map \Pr {A \cap B}$.
fields.explanation: The full source defines conditional probability with division by Pr(B), but proof line7 then explicitly identifies conditional probability with the unnormalized intersection probability. Only line7 is refuted; the chain rule and displayed theorem remain true. Keep the original four equally likely outcomes, A={1}, B={1,2}. Pr(B)=1/2 is positive, Pr(A intersection B)=1/4, and Pr(A given B)=1/2. An actual Mathlib probability measure is a weighted sum of four Dirac measures on Fin4. IsProbabilityMeasure is proved, the events are measurable, and Mathlib conditional measure evaluates to1/2, distinct from intersection measure1/4.
fields.flaw: If B is known to have occurred, the conditional probability of A given B equals Pr(A ∩ B).
fields.problem:
Title: Chain Rule for Probability/Proof

Let $\EE$ be an [[Definition:Experiment|experiment]] with [[Definition:Probability Space|probability space]] $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$.

Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be [[Definition:Event|events]] of $\EE$ such that $\map \Pr B > 0$.

The '''[[Definition:Conditional Probability|conditional probability of $A$ given $B$]]''' is:

:$\condprob A B = \dfrac {\map \Pr {A \cap B} } {\map \Pr B}$
fields.source_context:
0001 | Suppose it is given that $B$ has [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]].
0002 | 
0003 | Then the [[Definition:Probability|probability]] of $A$ having [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]] may not be $\map \Pr A$ after all.
0004 | 
0005 | In fact, we ''can'' say that $A$ has [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]] {{iff}} $A \cap B$ has [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]].
0006 | 
0007 | So, if we ''know'' that $B$ has [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]], the [[Definition:Conditional Probability|conditional probability]] of $A$ given $B$ is $\map \Pr {A \cap B}$.
0008 | 
0009 | It follows then, that:
0010 | :if we ''don't'' actually know whether $B$ has [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]] or not
0011 | :but we know its [[Definition:Probability|probability]] $\map \Pr B$
0012 | we can say that:
0013 | 
0014 | :The [[Definition:Probability|probability]] that $A$ and $B$ have both [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]] is the [[Definition:Conditional Probability|conditional probability]] of $A$ given $B$ [[Definition:Real Multiplication|multiplied]] by the [[Definition:Probability|probability]] that $B$ has [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]].
0015 | 
0016 | Hence:
0017 | :$\condprob A B = \dfrac {\map \Pr {A \cap B} } {\map \Pr B}$
0018 | {{qed}}
0019 |
fields.witness: Let Ω={1,2,3,4} with the uniform probability measure. Take A={1} and B={1,2}. Then Pr(B)=2/4=1/2>0, so conditioning is defined. Also A∩B={1}, hence Pr(A∩B)=1/4, while Pr(A|B)=Pr(A∩B)/Pr(B)=(1/4)/(1/2)=1/2. Thus Pr(A|B)≠Pr(A∩B).

scope_metadata.clarification: The counterexample concerns the local equality when Pr denotes the original probability measure. The final identity Pr(A|B)=Pr(A intersect B)/Pr(B) is not refuted.
scope_metadata.target_scope: Literal equality of conditional probability and the original probability of the intersection; not the normalized chain-rule formula printed at the end.
